## Dataset: The usage of landscape ecological concepts in the planning literature

Table of content: 1. Frequency of early concepts; 2. Frequency of additional concepts; 3. Use of any early concept; 4. Use of any additional concept, 5. Planning steps; 6. Protocol.<br>The present dataset is part of the published scientific paper entitled “Landscape ecological concepts in planning: review of recent developments” &#40;Hersperger et al., 2021&#41;. The goal of this research was to review recent publications to assess the use of landscape ecological concepts in planning. Specifically, we address the following research questions: Q1. Landscape ecological concepts: What are they? How frequently are they mentioned in current research? Q2. How are landscape ecological concepts integrated in landscape planning? <br>We analysed all empirical and overview papers that have been published in four key academic journals in the field of landscape ecology and landscape planning in the years 2015–2019 &#40;n = 1918&#41;. Four key journals in the field of landscape ecology were selected to conduct the analysis, respectively Landscape Ecology &#40;LE&#41;, Landscape Online &#40;LO&#41;, Current Landscape Ecology Reports &#40;CLER&#41;, and Landscape and Urban Planning &#40;LUP&#41;. The title, abstract and keywords of all papers were read in order to identify landscape ecological concepts. Then, all 1918 papers went through a keyword search to identify the use of early and additional concepts. We used the “pdfsearch” package in R programming language and searched for singular and plural forms and different variations of the concepts &#40;see Supplementary material 1, Table A&#41;. As a result, we provided four outputs: <br>&amp;nbsp; 1. Frequency of early concepts. This data provides the total number of times each article used each early concept &#40;Q1&#41;. This data was used to produce the Figure 2a at the original publication.<br>&amp;nbsp; 2. Frequency of additional concepts. This data provides the total number of times each article used each additional concept &#40;Q1&#41;. This data was used to produce the Figure 2b at the original publication.<br>&amp;nbsp; 3. Use of any early concept. This data provides the total number of times each article used any early concept &#40;Q1&#41;. <br>This data was used to produce the Figure 3a at the original publication.<br>&amp;nbsp; 4. Use of any additional concept. This data provides the total number of times each article used any additional concept &#40;Q1&#41;. This data was used to produce the Figure 3b at the original publication.   <br>To address the second question &#40;Q2&#41;, the title, abstract and keywords of the papers included in our sample &#40;n=1918 articles&#41; were screened to identify papers that might show how landscape ecological concepts are integrated into planning. We selected 52 empirical papers &#40;see Supplementary material – 4 Integration of landscape ecological concepts into planning&#41;, and we provided two outputs:<br>&amp;nbsp; 5. Planning steps.  This data provides the number of times landscape ecological concepts were addressed in each <br>planning steps in 52 empirical papers analysed in detail &#40;Q2&#41;. This data was used to produce the Figure 4 at the <br>original publication.<br>&amp;nbsp; 6. Protocol for assessing the integration of landscape ecological concepts into planning. To systematically collect the <br>data, we used this protocol which addressed the following questions: &#40;a&#41; which type of planning is addressed by the <br>paper? &#40;b&#41; to which planning level does the paper refer to? &#40;c&#41; which concepts are integrated in any of the planning <br>steps described above?

## Load packages

This template targets tidyverse (2.x) and skimr (2.x) with R 4.1 or newer for the native `|>` pipe; package versions are not pinned. Install missing packages once with `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "skimr"))`.

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
theme_set(theme_minimal())

USER_AGENT <- "OpendataSwiss-StarterCode-R/1.0"
HTTP_TIMEOUT <- 30

get_dataset <- function(url, delim = NULL, drop_empty_unnamed = TRUE, ...) {
  if (grepl("^https?://", url)) {
    local_file <- tempfile()
    on.exit(unlink(local_file), add = TRUE)
    old_options <- options(timeout = HTTP_TIMEOUT)
    on.exit(options(old_options), add = TRUE)
    status <- download.file(url, local_file, method = "libcurl", mode = "wb",
                            quiet = TRUE, headers = c("User-Agent" = USER_AGENT))
    if (status != 0) stop("Resource download failed")
    url <- local_file
  }
  data <- read_delim(url, delim = delim, show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
  stop_for_problems(data)
  if (drop_empty_unnamed && nrow(data) > 0) {
    # Blank CSV headers (often from trailing separators) become "...n".
    unnamed <- grepl("^\\.\\.\\.[0-9]+$", names(data))
    empty_unnamed <- unnamed & map_lgl(data, ~ all(is.na(.x)))
    if (any(empty_unnamed)) {
      message("Removed empty unnamed columns: ", paste(names(data)[empty_unnamed], collapse = ", "))
      data <- data[, !empty_unnamed, drop = FALSE]
    }
  }
  data
}
```

## Missing values

```{r missing-values}
missing <- tibble(
  column = names(df),
  missing = map_int(df, ~ sum(is.na(.x))),
  missing_pct = map_dbl(df, ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)
) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_pct))
missing

# Show up to 20 columns with missing values; percentages use all rows.
missing_plot <- missing |> filter(missing > 0) |> slice_head(n = 20)
if (nrow(missing_plot) > 0) {
  ggplot(missing_plot, aes(x = missing_pct, y = reorder(column, missing_pct))) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 100)) +
    labs(x = "Missing values (%)", y = NULL, title = "Missingness by column")
} else {
  message("No missing values to plot (or the dataset has no rows).")
}
```

`skim()` reports completeness and type-specific summaries. Inspect units before interpreting numeric codes as measurements.

```{r histograms}
# Plot up to four numeric columns, excluding non-finite values only from plots.
numeric_names <- names(select(df, where(is.numeric))) |> head(4)
for (column in numeric_names) {
  values <- df[[column]]
  values <- values[is.finite(values)]
  if (length(values) > 0) {
    plot <- ggplot(tibble(value = values), aes(x = value)) +
      geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "steelblue", colour = "white") +
      labs(title = column, x = column, y = "Count")
    print(plot)
  }
}
```

```{r category-counts}
# Top 10 values for up to three categorical columns, including missing values.
categorical_names <- df |>
  select(where(~ is.character(.x) || is.factor(.x) || is.logical(.x))) |>
  names() |>
  head(3)
for (column in categorical_names) {
  cat(column, "\n")
  df |> count(.data[[column]], sort = TRUE) |> head(10) |> print()
}
```
